title: The Anatomy of Strategy
author: Mr. Nickhart
summary: Mr. Nickhart provides a worked example of how he structures school improvement strategy, organised around four foundational concepts: strategic intent, a cohesive hierarchy, culture, and continuous checking. He begins from Vivianne Robinson's caution that designing the future before understanding the present leads to misdirected resources. Strategic intent, in his school's case, is embodied in the 'horizon' metaphor -- continuous improvement toward a moving target -- and three 'horizons': a flourishing school, an evolving curriculum, and serving community. The article maps how strategy, systems, culture-setting, and capacity-building each decompose differently at SLT, subject leader, and year-leader levels, and argues that trust is the prior condition without which none of the above functions.
points: Strategy must begin with accurate sense-making of the present, not projection of the future -- and the quality of that sense-making depends partly on the leader's stage of adult ego development, which shapes how they interpret complex situations.

A strategic narrative (a compelling metaphor or story) is more effective than a boxy improvement plan because stories drive behaviour and are memorable; the school described uses the horizon and stream metaphors to sustain coherence.

A cohesive hierarchy requires different types of actions at each leadership level (SLT, subject leaders, year leaders) across four dimensions -- strategy, systems, culture, and capacity-building -- preventing either disconnect or blurred accountability.

Trust is the precondition of all school improvement: 'There can be no improvement without trusting relationships and trust requires everyone to feel psychologically safe'; leaders must be attuned to behaviours that erode it and respond explicitly.

Informal learning (incidental, unplanned, occurring as a byproduct of daily work) is far more prevalent than formal CPD and constitutes a larger share of how teachers actually develop -- leaders therefore need to intentionally design the conditions for informal as well as formal learning.
quotes: Designing the future before understanding the present can lead to misdiagnosing the school's needs and in turn misdirecting attention and resources.

What is more compelling than a narrative. Stories drive behaviour and are memorable; finding the right narrative for the school community to bring to life the improvement works at the heart of school leadership.

The horizon is the furthest point that we can see, where the known meets the unknown, but horizons keep moving the closer we get. This is how we think about school improvement: no matter how good our provision, it can always be better.
There can be no improvement without trusting relationships and trust requires everyone to feel psychologically safe.
Truth does not rise to the top. Whatever our own experiences of the school, they are unlikely to be the lived reality because our colleagues are likely to want to show us the best of themselves.
Informal learning is far more prevalent than formal learning and there are many more opportunities for us to influence learning that than the regular, formal CPD sessions that we organise each week.
